Isaac Brock told Far Out Magazine in 2021 that finding Pixies' Doolittle in eighth grade gave him everything he wanted from a record -- hypnotic, deeply strange, with lyrics he could read a dozen ways.

Isaac Brock has described More Songs About Buildings and Food as the record that made him notice production at all -- he had heard it about forty thousand times before he started listening to how it was made.

Sharon Van Etten told the Irish Times in August 2025 that she listened to "dandies of doom" as an angst-ridden adolescent, including the Cure, Joy Division and Nine Inch Nails, recalling shutting her bedroom door and upsetting her mother; Billboard reported in January 2025 that her Attachment Theory demos read as UK-influenced, citing Joy Division and Kate Bush.

When producer John Congleton asked Sharon Van Etten about her influences before Remind Me Tomorrow (2019), she named Nick Cave's Skeleton Tree; Stereogum separately put to her that Cave was a big influence on the record, which she didn't dispute. She has repeated the connection across at least six interviews, including Billboard.

Tim Gane, Tape Op #98: "in the early and mid-'80s he was a big fan of krautrock music -- like Faust, Neu! and Can." Corroborated by ele-king: early records "infused with a gushing enthusiasm for Neu!'s motorik rhythms."

Tape Op #98; Electronic Sound dates the epiphany precisely to a 1980 Sounds review of a Faust reissue, which Tim Gane says "knocked him out."

Electronic Sound, Tim Gane: on why the Faust review landed, "he was a big fan of bands like Cabaret Voltaire, so his ears had already been opened to bolder, more experimental electronic music." New edge.
David Yow: the band was "four white guys who liked to play a cross between Led Zeppelin and the Birthday Party."

Duane Denison, guitarguitar.co.uk (Apr 2, 2021): compositional approach drew on "bands of the US underground scenes like Black Flag, Husker Du, Butthole Surfers and Big Black."

Tape Op, Geoff Stanfield (May 2023). Molly Rankin on writing "Pressed": "We were trying to do a Smiths' verse and an R.E.M. chorus, and then it morphs into whatever it is by the end of the song." Producer Shawn Everett confirms it in the same interview -- "They were going for The Smiths' reference."

Ilana Kaplan, SPIN (11 Mar 2015) and Rebecca Schiller, Diffuser.fm (21 Nov 2014) independently list Cocteau Twins among Molly Rankin's named influences. Asked separately by Pitchfork to name a perfect 10 album, she chose their Heaven or Las Vegas -- "I think it flows very well and it's also just otherworldly beauty and also menacing at the same time" -- which speaks to how deeply she holds the record rather than to influence on its own.

Asked by Allston Pudding who she had been listening to while making Alvvays' debut, Molly Rankin said she had little young influence growing up somewhere with no record store within two hours, but that at university she discovered "typical seminal bands The Replacements and The Smiths."
Stereogum "Under The Influence," Rachel Brodsky (3 Oct 2022). Molly Rankin: "I know Al has a lot of love for Yo La Tengo, as do I. I've seen them performing in many formations."

Tape Op, Geoff Stanfield (May 2023). Alec O'Hanley: "One thing we loved about Kevin Shields was the limitations he put on his stuff that's My Bloody Valentine" -- discussed as a working method, down to reusing the reverse reverb on a Yamaha SPX90.

Asked by KEXP what appeals to her as a songwriter about Camera Obscura, Molly Rankin said Tracyanne Campbell is "so good at longing and poetry and being endearing without being annoying," with a voice that's "so unique and pure." In a separate SPIN interview, Rankin called Camera Obscura's polish "a really nice reference" next to Alvvays' sparser, tape-hiss sound.

CityBeat: Marshall saw the Replacements in high school and watched Paul Westerberg come out alone at the end to sing "Answering Machine," throwing his guitar off his body and running -- "It impacted me so much." She later covered the song on Covers.
CityBeat interview: Marshall on Nico breaking the mould as a female icon -- "That European classical way of singing... is very influential."
